    "Youth and development": r"youth|\bltad\b|long[ _-]term[ _-]athlete|adolescen|maturation|\bphv\b",
}
RULES = {k: re.compile(v, re.I) for k, v in DISCIPLINES.items()}

# Named collections worth tracking as units. TB and Landon come from the manifest's
# collections column (it follows every duplicate copy); the rest match on path.
COLLECTIONS = {
    "Mike Golden library": r"Golden, Mike",
    "Old Bull Performance": r"old ?bull",
    "Harries On-Field RTP (Sportsmith)": r"SS_Course_OnFieldRTP",
    "CVASPS": r"cvasp",
    "ALTIS": r"altis",
    "Charlie Francis": r"charlie ?francis",
}
COLLECTION_RULES = {k: re.compile(v, re.I) for k, v in COLLECTIONS.items()}

# Eric's own generated reports and dashboards: a record of practice, not literature.
OWN_REPORTS = re.compile(r"DASHBOARDS_AND_REPORTS|Report_Templates", re.I)


def route(row: dict) -> str:
    if OWN_REPORTS.search(row["path"]):
        return "Eric's reports (archive)"
    kind, size = row["kind"], int(row["size"] or 0)
    if kind in ("video", "audio"):
        return "transcription queue"
    if kind == "paper_or_book":
        if row["ext"] in ("epub", "mobi") or size >= 8_000_000:
            return "book (ingest-book, gated)"
        return "paper (Zotero)"
    if kind in ("document", "slides"):
        return "vault atomize"
    if kind == "data":
        return "template or data (review)"
    return "catalog only"


def main() -> None:
    with open(DATA / "manifest.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig") as fh:
        rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(fh) if r["canonical"] == "True"]
    out, unclassified = [], []
    for r in rows:
        text = f"{r['source']}/{r['path']}".replace("_", " ")
        rt = route(r)
        # Reports keep no discipline tags so they do not inflate the literature counts.
        tags = [] if rt == "Eric's reports (archive)" else [k for k, rx in RULES.items() if rx.search(text)]
        colls = [c for c in (r.get("collections") or "").split(";") if c]
        colls += [k for k, rx in COLLECTION_RULES.items() if rx.search(text)]
        r = {**r, "disciplines": ";".join(tags), "route": rt, "collections": ";".join(sorted(set(colls)))}
        out.append(r)
        if not tags and rt != "Eric's reports (archive)":
            unclassified.append(r)
    fields = list(out[0])
    for name, subset in (("triage.csv", out), ("unclassified.csv", unclassified)):
        with open(DATA / name, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=fields)
            w.writeheader()
            w.writerows(subset)

    disc = Counter(t for r in out for t in r["disciplines"].split(";") if t)
    routes = Counter(r["route"] for r in out)
    lines = [
        "# Flint triage summary (rules pass)", "",
        f"Unique files: {len(out)}. Classified by rules: {len(out) - len(unclassified)} "
        f"({100 * (len(out) - len(unclassified)) / len(out):.0f}%). Unclassified: {len(unclassified)}.",
        "A file can carry several disciplines, so discipline counts sum to more than the file count.", "",
        "## By discipline", "", "| Discipline | Files | Papers/books | Video/audio |", "|---|---:|---:|---:|",
    ]
    for k, n in disc.most_common():
        sub = [r for r in out if k in r["disciplines"].split(";")]
        pb = sum(r["kind"] == "paper_or_book" for r in sub)
        av = sum(r["kind"] in ("video", "audio") for r in sub)
        lines.append(f"| {k} | {n} | {pb} | {av} |")
    lines += ["", "## By route", "", "| Route | Files |", "|---|---:|"]
    lines += [f"| {k} | {n} |" for k, n in routes.most_common()]
    coll = Counter(c for r in out for c in r["collections"].split(";") if c)
    lines += ["", "## Named collections", "", "| Collection | Files | Papers/books | Video/audio |", "|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for k, n in coll.most_common():
        sub = [r for r in out if k in r["collections"].split(";")]
        pb = sum(r["kind"] == "paper_or_book" for r in sub)
        av = sum(r["kind"] in ("video", "audio") for r in sub)
        lines.append(f"| {k} | {n} | {pb} | {av} |")
    (DATA / "triage_summary.md").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("\n".join(lines))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Reads data/manifest.csv, writes data/triage.csv (all unique files) and

    "Injury risk and prevention": r"injur|prevention|\bacwr\b|nordic|nordbord|screen|\bfms\b|risk",
    "Load monitoring and GPS": r"workload|training[ _-]load|\bload\b|\bgps\b|monitor|\brpe\b|wellness|\bhrv\b|fatigue|readiness|monotony|strain|acute|chronic",
    "Testing and assessment": r"force[ _-]?plate|\bcmj\b|countermovement|jump|testing|assessment|benchmark|profil|f-?v\b|force[ _-]velocity|\bvald\b|hawkin|isokinetic|\bimtp\b|\bdsi\b|\brsi\b|\bpca\b|combine|pro ?day",

    "Periodization and programming": r"periodi|programm|annual[ _-]plan|\bblock\b|macrocycle|mesocycle|taper|verkhoshansk|bondarchuk|issurin|matveyev|bompa|zatsiorsk|siff|supertraining|planning|planner|template|yessis|windows of trainability",

# collections column (it follows every duplicate copy); the rest match on path.
COLLECTIONS = {
    "Mike Golden library": r"Golden, Mike",
    "Old Bull Performance": r"old ?bull",
    "Harries On-Field RTP (Sportsmith)": r"SS.Course.OnFieldRTP",
    "CVASPS": r"cvasp",
    "ALTIS": r"altis",
    "Charlie Francis": r"charlie ?francis",
}
COLLECTION_RULES = {k: re.compile(v, re.I) for k, v in COLLECTIONS.items()}

# Eric's own generated reports and dashboards: a record of practice, not literature.
OWN_REPORTS = re.compile(r"DASHBOARDS_AND_REPORTS|Report_Templates", re.I)


def route(row: dict) -> str:
    if OWN_REPORTS.search(row["path"]):
        return "Eric's reports (archive)"
    kind, size = row["kind"], int(row["size"] or 0)
    if kind in ("video", "audio"):
        return "transcription queue"
    if kind == "paper_or_book":
        if row["ext"] in ("epub", "mobi") or size >= 8_000_000:
            return "book (ingest-book, gated)"

        return "vault atomize"
    if kind == "data":
        return "template or data (review)"
    return "catalog only"


def main() -> None:
    with open(DATA / "manifest.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig") as fh:
        rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(fh) if r["canonical"] == "True"]

    for r in rows:
        text = f"{r['source']}/{r['path']}".replace("_", " ")

        colls = [c for c in (r.get("collections") or "").split(";") if c]
        colls += [k for k, rx in COLLECTION_RULES.items() if rx.search(text)]
        r = {**r, "disciplines": ";".join(tags), "route": rt, "collections": ";".join(sorted(set(colls)))}
        out.append(r)
        if not tags and rt != "Eric's reports (archive)":
            unclassified.append(r)
    fields = list(out[0])
    for name, subset in (("triage.csv", out), ("unclassified.csv", unclassified)):
        with open(DATA / name, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=fields)
            w.writeheader()
            w.writerows(subset)

    disc = Counter(t for r in out for t in r["disciplines"].split(";") if t)
    routes = Counter(r["route"] for r in out)
    reports = sum(r["route"] == "Eric's reports (archive)" for r in out)
    lit = len(out) - reports
    lines = [
        "# Flint triage summary (rules pass)", "",
        f"Unique files: {len(out)}, of which {reports} are Eric's own reports and dashboards (archived, not classified). "
        f"Of the other {lit}, the rules classified {lit - len(unclassified)} ({100 * (lit - len(unclassified)) / lit:.0f}%); "
        f"{len(unclassified)} are left for the model pass (`data/unclassified.csv`).",
        "A file can carry several disciplines, so discipline counts sum to more than the file count.", "",
        "## By discipline", "", "| Discipline | Files | Papers/books | Video/audio |", "|---|---:|---:|---:|",
    ]
    for k, n in disc.most_common():
        sub = [r for r in out if k in r["disciplines"].split(";")]
        pb = sum(r["kind"] == "paper_or_book" for r in sub)
        av = sum(r["kind"] in ("video", "audio") for r in sub)
        lines.append(f"| {k} | {n} | {pb} | {av} |")
    lines += ["", "## By route", "", "| Route | Files |", "|---|---:|"]
    lines += [f"| {k} | {n} |" for k, n in routes.most_common()]
    coll = Counter(c for r in out for c in r["collections"].split(";") if c)
    lines += ["", "## Named collections", "", "| Collection | Files | Papers/books | Video/audio |", "|---|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for k, n in coll.most_common():
        sub = [r for r in out if k in r["collections"].split(";")]
        pb = sum(r["kind"] == "paper_or_book" for r in sub)
        av = sum(r["kind"] in ("video", "audio") for r in sub)
        lines.append(f"| {k} | {n} | {pb} | {av} |")
    (DATA / "triage_summary.md").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print("\n".join(lines))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Zotero backlog classification

Second item in the capability map's sequence, after the skill router. Every research
record in the Zotero library gets a topic; when Jev is not confident enough to name
one, it reports the broader domain that topic sits in instead. Nothing is dropped and
nothing queues for review.

Built 2026-09-19 from the `classification_using_confidence` cookbook
(`docs/vendor/typesafe/cookbooks/classification_using_confidence.md`). Code in
`zotero_classify/`.

**Governance: tier A.** Published literature and its metadata only. No athlete data,
no health records, nothing from GPS, force plate, DEXA or S2. The state sent to the
API is a title, a journal, a year and up to 2,000 characters of a published abstract.

## What came out

| | |
|---|---|
| records classified | **1,418** — every eligible research item, reconciled against the bridge's own count |
| named a specific topic | **1,236 (87%)** |
| reported as a domain instead | 182 (13%) |
| taxonomy | 96 topics in 14 domains |
| wall time | **86 seconds**, 8 workers, zero failures |
| cost | about **$0.07** at $0.042 per million input tokens, output free |

Deliverables, regenerate with `python export.py`:

- `zotero_classify/out/zotero_topics.csv` — one row per record: label, how specific it
  is, confidence, and whether it had an abstract. Sorts and filters in a spreadsheet.
- `zotero_classify/out/LIBRARY_MAP.md` — the library as a map, every domain and topic
  with counts and real example titles under each.

The library, by domain:

| Domain | Records |
|---|---:|
| testing-and-assessment | 204 |
| athletic-performance-training | 202 |
| biomechanics | 162 |
| athletic-medicine-injury-rtp | 161 |
| athlete-monitoring-and-load | 127 |
| motor-learning-and-skill | 127 |
| recovery-and-physiology | 90 |
| data-methods-and-technology | 71 |
| sport-performance-and-tactics | 61 |
| adjacent-and-foundational | 56 |
| nutrition-and-supplementation | 50 |
| profession-and-practice | 42 |
| psychology-and-behaviour | 40 |
| not-a-research-record | 25 |

That last row is a side benefit: 25 records whose title is a bare citation
(`Mann and Herman (1985)`), a filename (`ECSS_E-Poster_Barcelona-2013_Abstr-ID-2143`)
or a personal note. They are worth cleaning up in Zotero directly.

## The cutoff is 0.50, not the cookbook's 0.90

Measured on 41 hand-labelled records (`python validate.py`), stratified 18 with an
abstract, 18 title-only and 5 junk.
=== RULE ===
### The rule this project earned, stated as a gate rather than a story

Every item that was measured moved, and every one moved *down*. Entity alignment was
ranked second and was withdrawn. PP_Recruiting offered two obvious fits that both
collapsed into code. The Zotero renames were recommended skip. `AUTO_ACCEPT` came in
at the cookbook's 0.90 and measured to 0.80; the Zotero cutoff came in at 0.90 and
measured to 0.50. That is not bad luck, it is a missing gate. **Build only where all
three hold:**

1. **The answer is genuinely fuzzy** — not a join, not a threshold, not a lookup.
2. **Something already consumes the answer.** No consumer, no build. This is the
   Zotero-renames test.
3. **A code baseline was measured first.** If deterministic code gets most of the way,
   the model is decoration.

Each withdrawn item failed a *different* one of these, which is why no single check
would have caught them. Entity alignment failed (1) — exact string equality settled
287 of 300 and fuzzy matching contributed zero settled pairs. The Zotero renames
failed (2). The prose-number work nearly failed (3) and was saved only because the
band was measured before and after.

### Answer-key audit: a required step in every pre-registered test (added 2026-09-26)

Three measurements found a bad answer key, not a bad model: the surgery count (17 by
regex, 22 under blind labels), the Evidence Library tags (the reviewed labels sided
with Jev on 5 of 8 rules-picks), and the spring notes (role words the labels missed).
The "Just Ask Jev" paper (arXiv 2609.29429) reports the same on three public
benchmarks. So every pre-registration now carries this step, written down before the
first call:

1. **Pull the confident disagreements.** Every item where Jev's probability clears the
   pre-registered confidence cut and its answer differs from the label. Fix the cut
   in the pre-registration, not after seeing results.
2. **Eric judges them blind.** Shuffle, hide which side said what, show only the input
   and the two answers. He marks label right, Jev right, or unclear.
3. **Report both scores.** The pre-registered score on the original labels decides
   pass or fail, and the bar never moves. The audited score is reported next to it,
   and the count of labels changed is a finding in its own right.
4. **Cap the audit.** At most 20 items. If there are more than 20 confident
   disagreements, audit a random 20 and report the rate. More than that is a label
   problem worth its own write-up.

What this is not: a way to rescue a failed test. A test that fails on the original
labels and passes on the audited ones is reported as FAIL, with the audit as the reason
to re-run against fresh labels.

# Jev Drive triage: pre-registration (DRAFT, awaiting Eric's approval of the bars)

Status: **draft**. Nothing below has been run. Once Eric approves the bars, this file
moves into `TypeSafe_Sandbox/docs/` and is committed there *before the first call*,
following that repo's convention. The commit hash then goes in the "Registered" line.

Registered: (commit hash, filled on approval)

## Question

Can Jev put the Drive files that Flint's keyword rules cannot place into the same
14 domains and 96 topics it already uses for the Zotero library, confidently enough
that Flint can route them without a person looking at each one?

## Why it passes the capability map's gate

1. **The answer is genuinely fuzzy.** Deciding which domain a coaching PDF belongs to,
   from its folder, name and first page, is not a join or a lookup.
2. **Something consumes the answer.** Flint's triage routes every file by domain into
   Zotero, the vault, the book queue or the transcription queue, and builds a tier-A
   shortlist per domain from it.
3. **A code baseline was measured first.** `scripts/triage_rules.py` (keyword rules)
   classified 59% of the 9,702 non-report files. The Zotero md5 match recovers real
   titles for a further share of the files named by Drive ID. The model pass is only
   for what code leaves.

## Taxonomy

Reuse `zotero_classify/`'s 14 domains and 96 topics unchanged, so Drive files and
Zotero records share one map. Pass or fail is judged at **domain** level. Topic-level
accuracy is reported but does not decide anything.

## Sample: 200 files, drawn before any call

From `Flint/data/triage.csv`, excluding Eric's own reports, images and archives:

- 100 from `unclassified.csv` (the rules found nothing)
- 100 from the rules-classified files, to measure the rules' own precision

Stratified by source root, seed fixed, list committed with this file.

## State sent to Jev

Folder path, file name, the Zotero title when the md5 match recovered one, and up to
2,000 characters of first-page text for PDFs, Word files and slides. Video and audio
send path and name only. For Drive files that are not synced locally (TB's Training
Info), the first page comes from a `gws` download into `Flint/staging/`.

## Questions

The `zotero_classify` Choice over topics, with domain fallback below the cutoff,
unchanged. Plus one Choice for the route: paper, book, course or lecture material,
coaching resource, Eric's own material, not sport science.

## Answer key

Claude labels all 200 blind to Jev's answers, from the same state Jev sees, before
the first Jev call. Eric then audits under the capability map's answer-key audit rule.

## Comparators on the same 200

- Keyword rules (already run; unclassified counts as a miss)
- Haiku, one call per file, same state, same taxonomy
- Codex, same

## Bars (Eric to approve; fixed at registration, never moved)

| Measure | Bar |
|---|---|
| Jev confident (at the Zotero-measured 0.50 cut) | at least 60% of the 200 |
| Jev domain accuracy on its confident answers | at least 90% |
| Jev versus Haiku, domain accuracy on Jev's confident subset | Jev at least equal |
| Cost for the 200 | reported, no bar (the Zotero run cost about $0.07 for 1,418) |

## Answer-key audit (required step)

Every item where Jev clears the 0.50 cut and disagrees with the answer key. Eric judges
them blind (shuffled, sides hidden), at most 20, with a random 20 if there are more.
The score on the original labels decides pass or fail. The audited score is reported
next to it.

## If it passes

Run Jev on the remaining unclassified files. Below-cut answers fall back to domain
level, and anything still ambiguous goes to Claude. Result feeds Flint's tier-A
shortlists.

## If it fails

Whichever comparator scored best does the pass. The result is written up in the
sandbox as a tenth entry on the capability map.

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# ///
"""Draw the 200-file sample for the pre-registered Jev triage test.

    uv run scripts/draw_jev_sample.py

100 files the keyword rules could not classify plus 100 they did, each half
stratified by source root with proportional allocation (largest remainder), seed
fixed. Excludes Eric's own reports, images, archives and files already in Zotero
(those already carry a Jev topic from zotero_classify). Writes data/jev_sample.csv.
The sample is drawn once, before any model call, and committed with the
pre-registration.
"""
import csv
import random
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

SEED = 20260926
PER_HALF = 100
DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
EXCLUDE_ROUTES = {"Eric's reports (archive)", "already in Zotero"}
EXCLUDE_KINDS = {"image", "archive"}


def stratified(rows: list[dict], n: int, rng: random.Random) -> list[dict]:
    by_source = defaultdict(list)
    for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["id"]):  # stable order before shuffling
        by_source[r["source"]].append(r)
    total = len(rows)
    quotas = {s: n * len(v) / total for s, v in by_source.items()}
    alloc = {s: int(q) for s, q in quotas.items()}
    for s in sorted(quotas, key=lambda s: quotas[s] - alloc[s], reverse=True)[: n - sum(alloc.values())]:
        alloc[s] += 1
    picked = []
    for s in sorted(by_source):
        pool = by_source[s][:]
        rng.shuffle(pool)
        picked += pool[: alloc[s]]
    return picked


def main() -> None:
    with open(DATA / "triage.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(fh)
                if r["route"] not in EXCLUDE_ROUTES and r["kind"] not in EXCLUDE_KINDS]
    unclassified = [r for r in rows if not r["disciplines"]]
    classified = [r for r in rows if r["disciplines"]]
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    sample = [{**r, "stratum": "unclassified"} for r in stratified(unclassified, PER_HALF, rng)]
    sample += [{**r, "stratum": "rules-classified"} for r in stratified(classified, PER_HALF, rng)]
    for i, r in enumerate(sample, 1):
        r["sample_id"] = f"S{i:03d}"
    fields = ["sample_id", "stratum", "id", "source", "path", "name", "kind", "ext", "size",
              "zotero_title", "disciplines", "route", "collections"]
    with open(DATA / "jev_sample.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(sample)
    print(f"pool: {len(unclassified)} unclassified, {len(classified)} rules-classified; drew {len(sample)} (seed {SEED})")
    for stratum in ("unclassified", "rules-classified"):
        counts = defaultdict(int)
        for r in sample:
            if r["stratum"] == stratum:
                counts[r["source"]] += 1
        print(stratum + ": " + ", ".join(f"{s} {n}" for s, n in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1])))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Drive triage: pre-registration

Tenth item measured against the capability map. Registered 2026-09-26, **before any
model call**. The registering commit is the one that adds this file. Bars approved by
Eric on 2026-09-26. Consumer: the Flint project (`erash11/Flint`), which builds Eric's
sport-science knowledge base from his Drive.

**Governance: tier A.** The state is a Drive folder path, a file name, and up to 2,000
characters of a document's first page. The documents are coaching and research
material: books, papers, course handouts and slides. No athlete data. Flint's catalog
excludes DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports before anything
reaches this test.

## Question

Can Jev put the Drive files that Flint's keyword rules cannot place into the Zotero
taxonomy (14 domains, 96 topics, `zotero_classify/taxonomy.py`), confidently enough
that Flint can route them without a person reading each one?

## Gate check (capability map, three conditions)

1. **Genuinely fuzzy.** Deciding a coaching PDF's domain from its folder, name and
   first page is not a join, a threshold or a lookup.
2. **A consumer exists.** Flint routes every file by domain: into Zotero, the vault,
   the book queue or the transcription queue. It also builds a per-domain shortlist
   of files to ingest in full.
3. **Code baseline measured first.** Flint's keyword rules (`Flint/scripts/triage_rules.py`)
   classified 5,714 of 9,712 non-report files (59%). An md5 match against Zotero's
   Drive attachment store placed 81 more. The model pass covers only what code leaves.

## Sample (committed here: `drive_triage/sample.csv`)

200 files drawn by `Flint/scripts/draw_jev_sample.py`, seed 20260926, before any call.

- 100 from the 3,548 files the rules could not classify.
- 100 from the 5,254 files the rules did classify. These also measure the rules' own
  precision.
- Each half is stratified by source root, with proportional allocation.
- Excluded: Eric's own reports and dashboards, images, archives, and files already in
  Zotero.

## State per file

Folder path, file name, and the Zotero title where the md5 match recovered one. For
PDFs, Word files and slides, add up to 2,000 characters of first-page text. Video and
audio send path and name only. Files that are not synced locally (TB's Training Info)
are fetched with `gws` into a gitignored staging folder. State is built by code before
the answer key is written, and it is identical for every model.

## Questions

1. **Topic.** The `zotero_classify` topic Choice, unchanged (`classify.question()`),
   with the same domain fallback.
2. **Route.** One new Choice:
   - a research paper
   - a book or book chapter
   - course or lecture material
   - a coaching resource (programs, drills, templates, presentations)
   - Eric's own work
   - not sport-science material

## Answer key

Claude labels all 200 (domain, topic, route) from the same state, blind to every
model's answers, before the first Jev call. The labels are committed before Jev runs.

## Comparators (same 200, same state, same taxonomy)

- Flint's keyword rules, already run. On the unclassified half they count as misses.
- Haiku: one call per file, forced to name a topic.
- Codex: the same.

## Bars (fixed here; they never move)

| Measure | Bar |
|---|---|
| Jev confident: topic probability at or above the measured 0.50 cut | at least 60% of the 200 (120 files) |
| Jev domain accuracy on its confident answers, against the answer key | at least 90% |
| Jev versus Haiku: domain accuracy on Jev's confident subset | Jev at least equal to Haiku |
| Cost for the 200 | reported, no bar |

**Pass requires all three bars.** Topic-level and route accuracy are reported without
bars. The answer key comes before the models run, and the models do not define it.

## Answer-key audit (required step, capability map 2026-09-26)

Pull every file where Jev clears the 0.50 cut and its domain differs from the answer
key. Eric judges them blind: shuffled, sides hidden, input and the two answers only.
He sees at most 20 (a random 20 if there are more). The score on the original labels
decides pass or fail; the audited score is reported next to it.

## Outcomes

- **Pass.** Jev runs on Flint's remaining unclassified files. Below-cut answers fall
  back to domain, and anything still ambiguous goes to Claude.
- **Fail.** The best comparator does the pass. The result is written up here as the
  tenth entry on the map.

# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)

Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

---

1:# Flint interview prep: decision rules
5:## Top 8 (highest priority, in order)
7:[Omitted long matching line]
8:2. **The mRSI daily-readiness rule.** You state that force-plate mRSI replaced subjective wellness surveys as your daily readiness marker because it's "objective, consistent, and actionable." What value or week-over-week change in mRSI actually triggers a training adjustment, and for whom?
9:3. **The test-retirement threshold.** You retired roster-wide NordBord testing and daily wellness surveys, each for a stated reason (time cost and staff turnover; athletes gaming the survey). Is there a general rule you'd apply to the next technology or protocol decision, or is each call made fresh?
10:4. **RTP decision ownership and criteria.** The Playbook says Applied Performance "supports" Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions. What specific criteria, battery, or sign-off do you actually use or contribute, and where does your input end and Athletic Medicine's begin?
11:5. **Department reporting model.** Is Applied Performance a peer discipline that enables Athletics Performance/Athletic Medicine/Nutrition (Playbook framing), or is it in-house programming support for the Athletics Performance staff (course-narration framing: "helping program and plan the training")? These may not actually conflict, but the documents state both.
12:6. **Coach's-eye versus objective-first.** The course material argues you don't need a fancy test if you have a good coach's eye, and criticizes load-monitoring culture for breeding fear-driven under-training. Your own writing moved the opposite way on daily monitoring, replacing subjective self-report with an objective force-plate number. Where do you actually draw that line?
13:7. **GPS/load thresholds per sport.** Your own gap analysis says the data dictionary has no sport-specific, contextualized thresholds yet. Do any exist informally, even if undocumented?
14:8. **Assessment Manual currency.** The AP Assessment Manual (V12) references GymAware and a contact-mat CMJ; the current stack centers on Perch and ForceDecks-only CMJ. Is the Manual current, partially superseded, or fully legacy?

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- Books go through the ingest review gate (automated check plus an independent falsifying review) before atomization.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-resource

# Ingest Resource

Turn any incoming resource into a well-placed, summarized, cross-linked vault note.

**Vault:** `vault_root` in the selected platform config
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.

## Process

### 1. Acquire the content

| Input | How to get content |
|-------|-------------------|
| Article URL | WebFetch first; if empty/JS-shell, use web-scraping skill's `firecrawl_scrape.py -o tmp.md` |
| YouTube link | WebFetch the page for title/channel/description; ask user to paste transcript if the content itself is needed |
| PDF | Read tool (use `pages` for long PDFs) |
| Pasted transcript / note | Already in hand |
| Local file path | Read it |

### 2. Route it

Decide by **shelf life**, not topic:

- **`Knowledge/`** — stable reference that will still be true in a year: frameworks, mental models, voice/style guides, people profiles, processes, how-tos. Subfolder by kind: `Knowledge/frameworks/`, `Knowledge/people/`, `Knowledge/processes/`, `Knowledge/voice/` (add others as needed).
- **`Projects/`** — fuel for active work: video research, newsletter material, launch assets, anything tied to a current effort. If it belongs to an existing project file/folder (`Project_*.md`, `Graphify/`, etc.), place it alongside; otherwise drop it in `Projects/` root with a clear name.

Create any folder that doesn't exist yet (`New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force`). If routing is genuinely ambiguous, ask one question; otherwise decide and say why.

### 3. Write the note

Filename: kebab-case slug of the title (vault convention). Format:

```markdown
---
type: resource
created: YYYY-MM-DD
source: <URL, "PDF: filename", or "conversation">
domain: [one, two]
tags: [three, four]
status: ingested
---

# Title

> **Summary**
> **Source:** <link or origin> · **Date:** <published or ingested date>
> **Key people:** [[Person One]], Person Two
> **Key concepts:** concept one, concept two, concept three
>
> 2–4 sentence digest of what this is and why it was kept.

<full content or distilled body>
```

### 4. Cross-link

- List existing note names: filenames (sans `.md`) across `Notes/`, `Knowledge/`, `Projects/`.
- In the new note's body, wikilink the **first mention** of any concept/person/project that matches an existing note: `[[adoption-is-the-bottleneck]]` or `[[Project_AI-Integration|AI Integration]]`.
- Link related-but-not-mentioned notes in a `## Related` section at the bottom (2–5 links max, only genuinely related).
- A `[[wikilink]]` to a note that doesn't exist yet is fine for key people/concepts worth a future note — use sparingly.

### 5. Confirm

Report: file path, route chosen (and why), links added. One short paragraph.

## Rules

- **Never overwrite** an existing note — if the slug collides, append `-2` or merge after asking.
- Long sources (>2,000 words): keep the full text in the body but make the summary block self-sufficient.
- Don't route to `Notes/` — that folder is for synthesized permanent notes (interview-me's territory), not raw resources.
- Don't route to `Inbox/` — ingestion IS the processing step; the note lands in its final home.

## Verification Gate

After writing the note:

1. Read it back and verify the destination path, route, frontmatter, summary block, full-source body, and related-links section are present as applicable.
2. Compare the summary with the source. Require all named people, numbers, dates, quotations, and conclusions to preserve the source's meaning and attribution.
3. Confirm the new note did not overwrite an unrelated file and that the final slug is unique.
4. Check each wikilink target. Existing-note links must resolve; intentional future-note links must be labeled as such in the verification result.

Report `PASS` only when the written note matches the source and all filesystem checks succeed. Report `FAIL` for missing source content, altered claims, an overwrite, or a broken link presented as existing. Report `DEGRADED` when the source could not be fully accessed and identify what was summarized from partial evidence.

# Case Study: An Elite Sprinter and a Hurdler on Run-Specific Isometrics

**What it is** — Natera presents two athletes (~93:07–101:49).

**Elite male sprinter.** He was a strong, "power-hungry" athlete: a good accelerator but poorly elastic, with a weak max velocity.
- **Baseline:** back squat about **2.65× BW**; isometric mid-thigh pull **5.78× BW**. It is unclear whether that was single- or double-leg; the pull came before Natera moved to iso squats. CMJ about **59–62 cm**.
- **GPP:** eccentric calf work, then hip ISO holds progressing to switches.
- **SPP:** ankle and hip ISO catches, plus "ISO stadium descents," a loaded, cyclical isometric step-down that comes after the continuum.
- **Loads cited:** ankle ISO catch "up to 160 kg" (the transcript says "leaving up to 160 kilo"), which is implausible against his own 60 kg example and needs verifying on video. Hip ISO catch about 35 kg.
- **Reported changes:** CMJ +3 cm; CMJ power (~6,000 W) +200–300 W; takeoff velocity up; **RSI** "improved significantly," which he calls the main win; shorter contact times at about 30–40 m; longer acceleration and higher max velocity (around 11 m/s).

**Female 100 m hurdler.** She was coached by a Polish coach whose name the ASR renders "Peter Marazu ski" (name unverified), with Natera collaborating. Her times stagnated in 2016–2017. Run-specific isometrics (RSI) were added in 2018 through mid-2019 alongside "track training" and traditional squats, deadlifts and Olympic lifts. She used **holds and pushes only**, and progressed past targets such as a **2× BW ankle hold**. Afterwards her hurdle times and speed improved to "elite level." Her quote to a reporter: "I don't lift heavy weights. I just hold them."

*(Every number is single-source ASR from slides; the before/after charts are visual only. Verify at ~95:05–100:58.)*

**Why it works** — Natera's interpretation: isometrics raised reactive strength without extra plyometric volume, and position-specific strength carried over into running. Neither interpretation can be separated from other causes in these data.

**When to apply** — Use the sprinter as a **profile template**, not as evidence: high max strength (squat ≥2.5× BW) plus a low RSI and poor max velocity is the athlete Natera would target. In football that is the big, strong accelerator (RB/LB type) whose drop-jump RSI on ForceDecks is low for his strength. Track RSI and single-leg iso push together to see whether one moves without the other.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** Each case is n = 1 with concurrent training: sprint coaching, traditional lifting, technical work and maturation. There is no control, and the selection is plainly of successes. The hurdler also had a new collaborating coach, "great coaching and great technical training," per Natera himself. Elsewhere (~34:19–35:15) he reports programs where RSI was "the only change," and he concedes that is "not exactly a controlled scientific experiment." Do not cite these cases as evidence that RSI improves sprint speed. The 160 kg ankle catch must not become a target.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book

# Ingest Book

Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.

**Library root:** `vault_library` in the selected platform config
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.

## Model split (cost vs quality)

This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
  doesn't compound across the book.

## Schema for every entry note

Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.

```yaml
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: <domain-slug>
book: <book-slug>
chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
topic: <2-5 word topic>
category: [tag, tag]
confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <Human title of the idea>

**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
**Example** — one concrete instance.
```

**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.

## Phase 1 — Intake

1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.

`_book.md` template:
```markdown
---
type: book-index
book: <book-slug>
title: <full title>
author: <author>
domain: <domain-slug>
ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <title> — ingest map

| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
|---|---------|--------|---------|
| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
```

## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)

**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
  confidence entries from a scanned file.
- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`). For each:
  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.

**Kindle highlights:**
- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".

**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
  confidence ≤ untested.

## Phase 3 — Quality gate (run before writing each batch)

- One idea per note. If an extracted point is compound, split it.
- "When NOT to apply" present and non-trivial.
- **Dedup + converge:** before writing, `memsearch search` the library for the same
  concept. If an existing entry (any book) covers it, DON'T duplicate — instead add a
  `[[wikilink]]` + one line to both notes recording the agreement, and only add a new
  note if it contributes a genuinely new angle.
- Never overwrite an existing file; on slug collision append `-2`.

## Phase 4 — Close-out

1. Set all done rows in `_book.md`; if partial, leave pending rows for next session.
2. Add the book to `_domain.md`'s `books:` list and the "Books in this domain" section.
3. Add the book-slug to the advisor persona's `books:` list (`advisors/<domain>.md`)
   if an advisor exists.
4. Run `memsearch index "<vault_library>"` using the selected platform config
   so entries are searchable immediately (don't wait for the SessionEnd hook).
5. Commit the vault using `vault_root` from the selected platform config: `git -C "<vault_root>" add Knowledge/library && git commit -m "ingest(<book-slug>): <N> entries, ch X-Y"`.
6. Report: entries by kind and confidence, links created, chapters remaining.

## Rules
- Raw book text stays in the sandbox; only atomized entries enter context/the vault.
- Resumable by design: `_book.md` is the source of truth for "where am I".
- A 300-page book is a multi-session job — stop at a chapter boundary, never mid-chapter.

# Review and Plan: Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation (Sportsmith)

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Written 2026-09-25. Private working document.

Source: Simon Harries, *The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation* (Sportsmith). Seven parts: seven PDFs plus seven videos, about 2 h 10 min in total. Every PDF and every transcript in this folder was read. The transcripts are machine speech-to-text checked against the player captions; nobody listened back to the audio. Two terms are still unclear, Part 3 at about 15:51 and Part 6 at about 02:24. They are left unclear here too.

## 1. What the course is

It is one AFL practitioner's framework for the bridge from gym to field. It has three parts:

- **Five levels.** Level 1 to Level 5, then a return to training.
- **Three pillars.** Linear running from submaximal to maximal velocity (MV), multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skill.
- **Two axes.** Intensity (competency, then capacity) and complexity (control, then chaos).

The course ends with a four-step recipe for building your own framework: levels, pillars, intensity factors, drill menu.

The numbers that make it worth owning come from the Part 3 transcript, because the PDF lost the table:

| Level | Target % of max velocity | Typical content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50–70% | Running prep drills (dribbles, A-skips, pogos, scissors); fixed-distance repeats with a time target (60 m in 13 → 12 → 11 s) |
| 2 | 70–75% | Faster 60 m repeats; COD under 45° |
| 3 | 75–85% | Broken strides: 20 m accelerate, 20 m hold, 20 m decelerate, with only the hold phase timed (e.g. 2.88–3.0 s ≈ 24–25 km/h); closed-reactive drills |
| 4 | 85–95% | Undulating sessions; flies; open-reactive drills; bigger spaces |
| 5 | >95–100% | Evasive and competitive work; repeat sprints (2 × 3–4 × 40 m, all >85% MV, one every 30 s) |

**The gate at 75–85% MV.** Before a player runs faster than this, the course checks four things:
- enough healing time;
- earlier sessions came back with minimal pain or awareness of the area;
- force benchmarks: Nordic at least 80–85% of the player's pre-injury value for hamstrings, seated calf isometric about 1.7–1.8× body weight for the calf;
- a reactive-strength hop test.

**The exit rule.** At least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% MV before return. He gives no fixed number and says it depends on context.

## 2. Objective opinion

**Verdict: worth keeping as a dosage reference. It is weak as a teaching model and not built for football. Take the numbers, not the theory.**

What is strong:

1. **Session-level numbers are rare, and this course has them.** The 60 m timed repeats, the broken-stride timing, the linear-then-undulating shift at about 80–85%, the 75–85% gate, and the repeat-sprint format can all be written into a plan tomorrow. Most RTP writing stops at "progress gradually."
2. **The intensity levers are the most useful single table in the course.** For multidirectional work he names eight dials: velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, preparation distance or time, space, reactivity, % effort, and % MV. He also points out that they interact: shrinking the space caps the entry speed. That gives you a checklist, not a feel.
3. **Intensity and complexity are separate axes.** He is explicit that a new level does not make every drill chaotic. Some actions stay controlled at high intensity while others are already in chaos. That is correct, and many practitioners get it wrong.
4. **The case studies are honest.**
   - Case 1 returned without ever exceeding 90% MV.
   - Case 2 returned a week before the staff recommendation.
   - Sprint volume was under-dosed at 40% of game value.
   - A low high-speed-running threshold (17 km/h) twice inflated the totals by accident.

   Real practice looks like this, and it shows where the framework bends.

What is weak:

1. **It is Matt Taberner's control-chaos continuum with a velocity layer added.** Harries credits Taberner himself. You already hold five Taberner papers (see `RTP_Constraints_Course/RESOURCES.md`). The course adds nothing new to the theory; its new value is the worked numbers.
2. **The complexity axis rests on older motor-learning theory, not ecological dynamics.** This matters most for Joe's course.
   - Blocked → serial → random practice is contextual interference, from the Schmidt information-processing tradition.
   - His "closed reactivity" example is a coach throwing a hand signal. That is a generic stimulus, not the information a player actually uses in a game, such as a defender's hips.
   - He mentions "constraints-based learning design" once, in Part 2, in one sentence, and never puts it into practice.
   - In this model, complexity is something added once intensity is safe. In an ecological model, the right information has to be present from the start and scaled, not switched on at Level 4.

# Review and Plan: Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation (Sportsmith)

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Written 2026-09-25. Private working document.

Source: Simon Harries, *The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation* (Sportsmith). Seven parts: seven PDFs plus seven videos, about 2 h 10 min in total. Every PDF and every transcript in this folder was read. The transcripts are machine speech-to-text checked against the player captions; nobody listened back to the audio. Two terms are still unclear, Part 3 at about 15:51 and Part 6 at about 02:24. They are left unclear here too.

## 1. What the course is

It is one AFL practitioner's framework for the bridge from gym to field. It has three parts:

- **Five levels.** Level 1 to Level 5, then a return to training.
- **Three pillars.** Linear running from submaximal to maximal velocity (MV), multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skill.
- **Two axes.** Intensity (competency, then capacity) and complexity (control, then chaos).

The course ends with a four-step recipe for building your own framework: levels, pillars, intensity factors, drill menu.

The numbers that make it worth owning come from the Part 3 transcript, because the PDF lost the table:

| Level | Target % of max velocity | Typical content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50–70% | Running prep drills (dribbles, A-skips, pogos, scissors); fixed-distance repeats with a time target (60 m in 13 → 12 → 11 s) |
| 2 | 70–75% | Faster 60 m repeats; COD under 45° |
| 3 | 75–85% | Broken strides: 20 m accelerate, 20 m hold, 20 m decelerate, with only the hold phase timed (e.g. 2.88–3.0 s ≈ 24–25 km/h); closed-reactive drills |
| 4 | 85–95% | Undulating sessions; flies; open-reactive drills; bigger spaces |
| 5 | >95–100% | Evasive and competitive work; repeat sprints (2 × 3–4 × 40 m, all >85% MV, one every 30 s) |

**The gate at 75–85% MV.** Before a player runs faster than this, the course checks four things:
- enough healing time;
- earlier sessions came back with minimal pain or awareness of the area;
- force benchmarks: Nordic at least 80–85% of the player's pre-injury value for hamstrings, seated calf isometric about 1.7–1.8× body weight for the calf;
- a reactive-strength hop test.

**The exit rule.** At least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% MV before return. He gives no fixed number and says it depends on context.

## 2. Objective opinion

**Verdict: worth keeping as a dosage reference. It is weak as a teaching model and not built for football. Take the numbers, not the theory.**

What is strong:

1. **Session-level numbers are rare, and this course has them.** The 60 m timed repeats, the broken-stride timing, the linear-then-undulating shift at about 80–85%, the 75–85% gate, and the repeat-sprint format can all be written into a plan tomorrow. Most RTP writing stops at "progress gradually."
2. **The intensity levers are the most useful single table in the course.** For multidirectional work he names eight dials: velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, preparation distance or time, space, reactivity, % effort, and % MV. He also points out that they interact: shrinking the space caps the entry speed. That gives you a checklist, not a feel.
3. **Intensity and complexity are separate axes.** He is explicit that a new level does not make every drill chaotic. Some actions stay controlled at high intensity while others are already in chaos. That is correct, and many practitioners get it wrong.
4. **The case studies are honest.**
   - Case 1 returned without ever exceeding 90% MV.
   - Case 2 returned a week before the staff recommendation.
   - Sprint volume was under-dosed at 40% of game value.
   - A low high-speed-running threshold (17 km/h) twice inflated the totals by accident.

   Real practice looks like this, and it shows where the framework bends.

What is weak:

1. **It is Matt Taberner's control-chaos continuum with a velocity layer added.** Harries credits Taberner himself. You already hold five Taberner papers (see `RTP_Constraints_Course/RESOURCES.md`). The course adds nothing new to the theory; its new value is the worked numbers.
2. **The complexity axis rests on older motor-learning theory, not ecological dynamics.** This matters most for Joe's course.
   - Blocked → serial → random practice is contextual interference, from the Schmidt information-processing tradition.
   - His "closed reactivity" example is a coach throwing a hand signal. That is a generic stimulus, not the information a player actually uses in a game, such as a defender's hips.
   - He mentions "constraints-based learning design" once, in Part 2, in one sentence, and never puts it into practice.
   - In this model, complexity is something added once intensity is safe. In an ecological model, the right information has to be present from the start and scaled, not switched on at Level 4.

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["faster-whisper>=1.0"]
# ///
"""Transcribe a lecture or talk to timestamped Markdown, locally, on CPU.

    uv run scripts/transcribe.py "<video or audio path>" [--model medium.en]

ffmpeg pulls a 16 kHz mono audio track into staging/audio/ first, so the (possibly
1 GB) video is read once. Output: staging/transcripts/<slug>.md with one line per
segment, "[mm:ss] text". This is machine speech-to-text: nobody has listened back, and
the header says so. Names and numbers need checking against slides before any entry
cites them.
"""
import argparse
import re
import subprocess
import time
from pathlib import Path

from faster_whisper import WhisperModel

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
AUDIO, OUT = ROOT / "staging" / "audio", ROOT / "staging" / "transcripts"


def slug(p: Path) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", p.stem.lower()).strip("-")


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("source")
    ap.add_argument("--model", default="medium.en")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    src = Path(a.source)
    AUDIO.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    wav = AUDIO / f"{slug(src)}.wav"
    if not wav.exists():
        subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-loglevel", "error", "-i", str(src), "-vn", "-ac", "1", "-ar", "16000", str(wav)], check=True)
    t0 = time.time()
    model = WhisperModel(a.model, device="cpu", compute_type="int8")
    segments, info = model.transcribe(str(wav), vad_filter=True, beam_size=5)
    lines = []
    for s in segments:
        m, sec = divmod(int(s.start), 60)
        lines.append(f"[{m:02d}:{sec:02d}] {s.text.strip()}")
    header = (f"---\nsource: {src}\nmodel: faster-whisper {a.model} (CPU, int8, VAD)\n"
              f"duration_min: {info.duration / 60:.1f}\nchecked: no (machine transcript, nobody listened back)\n---\n\n")
    out = OUT / f"{slug(src)}.md"
    out.write_text(header + "\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"{out}  {info.duration / 60:.1f} min audio, {len(lines)} segments, {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min to transcribe")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Flint ingest queue

The order in which sources go into the vault library. Each course or book is atomized
by Sonnet into `staging/library/` and reviewed by Codex against its source, following
the ingest review gate. Only then is it copied into SecondBrain, indexed and committed.

## In progress

1. **Harries, The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation** (Sportsmith).
   - Domain: new `rehab-and-return-to-play`. Book slug: `on-field-rtp--harries`.
   - Stance: Eric's 2026-09-25 review. Keep it as a dosage reference; the theory is Taberner's control-chaos continuum with a velocity layer.
2. **Old Bull Performance course**.
   - Domain: new `performance-technology-and-leadership`. Book slug: `old-bull-performance-course--old-bull`.

## Next: Landon Evans (queued 2026-09-26 by Eric)

681 unique files. Most of it is a curated library Landon gave Eric (`From Landon Evans/Eric Files/`), not Landon's own writing. Landon's own teaching goes first, because it is his voice that gets compared with Eric's method.

- ALTIS / Ken Clark articles, into Zotero.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- Books go through the ingest review gate (automated check plus an independent falsifying review) before atomization.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

import logging, re
from pathlib import Path
from pypdf import PdfReader

logging.disable(logging.WARNING)
b = Path(r"G:\My Drive\Athletic Performance & Sports Science\Shared Reference Library\From Landon Evans\Eric Files\Physical Preparation")
for f in [b / "Books/Block Periodization - Issurin.pdf",

    r = PdfReader(str(f)); n = len(r.pages)

The order in which sources go into the vault library. Each course or book is atomized

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

# Flint ingest queue

The order in which sources go into the vault library. Each course or book is atomized
by Sonnet into `staging/library/` and reviewed by Codex against its source, following
the ingest review gate. Only then is it copied into SecondBrain, indexed and committed.

## In progress

1. **Harries, The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation** (Sportsmith).
   - Domain: new `rehab-and-return-to-play`. Book slug: `on-field-rtp--harries`.
   - Stance: Eric's 2026-09-25 review. Keep it as a dosage reference; the theory is Taberner's control-chaos continuum with a velocity layer.
2. **Old Bull Performance course**.
   - Domain: new `performance-technology-and-leadership`. Book slug: `old-bull-performance-course--old-bull`.

## Next: Landon Evans (queued 2026-09-26 by Eric)

681 unique files. Most of it is a curated library Landon gave Eric (`From Landon Evans/Eric Files/`), not Landon's own writing. Landon's own teaching goes first, because it is his voice that gets compared with Eric's method.

| Step | What | Files | Route |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | His *Elite Sports Performance* course: Units 1 to 4 lecture slides, plus the fuller Evans Unit 3 set (lectures 1 to 8, with an exam study guide) | about 30 PDFs | Atomize as a course (`elite-sports-performance--evans`). The slides are text but sparse (22 to 45 words a page), so slide-only entries are capped at `untested` |
| L2 | His talks: CVASPS "Physical Preparation in the NCAA: A Complementary Approach" (1 GB video, plus a CVASPS mp3), and the 2014 Boston "Performance Analytics" slides | 3 | Transcribe the CVASPS talk first in the transcription queue. Where the talk matches an L1 entry, raise that entry to `supported` |
| L3 | Therapy folder: fills the rehab gap next to Harries | 46 papers, 17 videos, 3 audio | Papers go to Zotero; video and audio go to the transcription queue |
| L4 | Training books (Verkhoshansky, Bondarchuk, Issurin, Zatsiorsky, Siff, Francis, and others) | 188 flagged as books | `ingest-book`, one at a time behind the gate. **First: *Supertraining*, started 2026-09-26 at Eric's call.** Source is the 6th Expanded single PDF from TB (591 pages, text, md5-verified), slug `supertraining--verkhoshansky`, domain strength-and-conditioning. Chapter map plus Chapter 1 are in progress; later chapters run one batch each. **Then Bondarchuk (queued by Eric 2026-09-26)**, in the order below |
| L5 | Papers in Physical Preparation, Science and Training Science | about 350 | Bulk import into Zotero, deduplicated against the library |
| L6 | Nutrition | 242 | Later. It is outside the current synthesis order |

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.13"
# dependencies = ["rapidocr-onnxruntime>=1.3", "pymupdf>=1.24", "numpy"]
# ///
"""OCR an image-only PDF into page-marked Markdown, locally, on CPU.

    uv run scripts/ocr_pdf.py "<pdf>" [--pages 1-10] [--dpi 200] [--out staging/ocr/<slug>.md]

Each page is rendered with PyMuPDF and read with RapidOCR (ONNX models, no admin, no
system install). Reading order: text boxes are grouped into lines by vertical
position. When a page has two columns, or is a two-page spread, the halves are read
left then right, detected from a clear vertical gutter. The output uses the same
"<!-- page N -->" markers as extract_text.py, so entries can cite PDF pages. A
companion CSV lists, per page, the words, box count and mean recognition confidence.
Pages below the confidence floor are listed at the end, so an atomizer checks them
against the page image and does not trust them blindly.
"""
import argparse
import csv
import re
import time
from pathlib import Path

import fitz  # PyMuPDF
import numpy as np
from rapidocr_onnxruntime import RapidOCR

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
LOW_CONF = 0.80


def parse_pages(spec: str | None, n: int) -> list[int]:
    if not spec:
        return list(range(1, n + 1))
    out = []
    for part in spec.split(","):
        a, _, b = part.partition("-")
        out += list(range(int(a), int(b or a) + 1))
    return [p for p in out if 1 <= p <= n]


def lines_from_boxes(boxes: list) -> list[str]:
    """Group OCR boxes into text lines, top to bottom, left to right."""
    items = []
    for pts, text, conf in boxes:
        ys = [p[1] for p in pts]; xs = [p[0] for p in pts]
        items.append((sum(ys) / 4, min(xs), max(ys) - min(ys), text))
    items.sort()
    lines, cur, cur_y, cur_h = [], [], None, 0
    for y, x, h, t in items:
        if cur_y is not None and abs(y - cur_y) > max(cur_h, h) * 0.6:
            lines.append(" ".join(t for _, t in sorted(cur))); cur = []
        cur.append((x, t)); cur_y = y if cur_y is None else (cur_y + y) / 2; cur_h = h
    if cur:
        lines.append(" ".join(t for _, t in sorted(cur)))
    return lines


def split_columns(boxes: list, width: float) -> list[list]:
    """Return [left, right] if a clear vertical gutter exists near the middle, else [boxes]."""
    if len(boxes) < 12:
        return [boxes]
    mid_lo, mid_hi = width * 0.42, width * 0.58
    best = None
    for gx in np.linspace(mid_lo, mid_hi, 17):
        crossing = sum(1 for pts, _, _ in boxes if min(p[0] for p in pts) < gx < max(p[0] for p in pts))
        if best is None or crossing < best[1]:
            best = (gx, crossing)
    gx, crossing = best
    left = [b for b in boxes if max(p[0] for p in b[0]) <= gx]
    right = [b for b in boxes if min(p[0] for p in b[0]) >= gx]
    if crossing <= max(1, len(boxes) * 0.03) and len(left) >= 5 and len(right) >= 5:
        return [left, right]
    return [boxes]


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("pdf")
    ap.add_argument("--pages")
    ap.add_argument("--dpi", type=int, default=200)
    ap.add_argument("--out")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    src = Path(a.pdf)
    slug = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", src.stem.lower()).strip("-")
    out = Path(a.out) if a.out else ROOT / "staging" / "ocr" / f"{slug}.md"
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    doc = fitz.open(src)
    pages = parse_pages(a.pages, doc.page_count)
    engine = RapidOCR()
    rows, parts, t0 = [], [], time.time()
    for pno in pages:
        page = doc[pno - 1]
        pix = page.get_pixmap(dpi=a.dpi)
        img = np.frombuffer(pix.samples, dtype=np.uint8).reshape(pix.height, pix.width, pix.n)
        if pix.n == 4:
            img = img[:, :, :3]
        result, _ = engine(img)
        boxes = result or []
        text_lines = []
        for col in split_columns(boxes, pix.width):
            text_lines += lines_from_boxes(col) + [""]
        body = "\n".join(text_lines).strip()
        confs = [float(c) for _, _, c in boxes]
        mean_conf = sum(confs) / len(confs) if confs else 0.0
        rows.append({"page": pno, "words": len(body.split()), "boxes": len(boxes), "mean_conf": round(mean_conf, 3)})
        parts.append(f"<!-- page {pno} -->\n{body}")
        print(f"page {pno}: {len(body.split())} words, conf {mean_conf:.2f}", flush=True)
    low = [r["page"] for r in rows if r["boxes"] and r["mean_conf"] < LOW_CONF]
    blank = [r["page"] for r in rows if r["boxes"] == 0]
    header = (f"---\nsource: {src}\nocr: RapidOCR (onnxruntime, CPU) at {a.dpi} dpi\npages: {len(pages)}\n"
              f"low_confidence_pages: {low}\nno_text_pages: {blank}\n"
              f"note: machine OCR. Check numbers, names and tables against the page image before citing.\n---\n\n")
    out.write_text(header + "\n\n".join(parts) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    with open(out.with_suffix(".csv"), "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        w.writeheader(); w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"{out}: {len(pages)} pages in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min; low-confidence {len(low)}, blank {len(blank)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
