# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.13"
# dependencies = ["rapidocr-onnxruntime>=1.3", "pymupdf>=1.24", "numpy"]
# ///
"""OCR an image-only PDF into page-marked Markdown, locally, on CPU.

    uv run scripts/ocr_pdf.py "<pdf>" [--pages 1-10] [--dpi 200] [--out staging/ocr/<slug>.md]

Each page is rendered with PyMuPDF and read with RapidOCR (ONNX models, no admin, no
system install). Reading order: text boxes are grouped into lines by vertical
position. When a page has two columns, or is a two-page spread, the halves are read
left then right, detected from a clear vertical gutter. The output uses the same
"<!-- page N -->" markers as extract_text.py, so entries can cite PDF pages. A
companion CSV lists, per page, the words, box count and mean recognition confidence.
Pages below the confidence floor are listed at the end, so an atomizer checks them
against the page image and does not trust them blindly.
"""
import argparse
import csv
import re
import time
from pathlib import Path

import fitz  # PyMuPDF
import numpy as np
from rapidocr_onnxruntime import RapidOCR

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
LOW_CONF = 0.80


def parse_pages(spec: str | None, n: int) -> list[int]:
    if not spec:
        return list(range(1, n + 1))
    out = []
    for part in spec.split(","):
        a, _, b = part.partition("-")
        out += list(range(int(a), int(b or a) + 1))
    return [p for p in out if 1 <= p <= n]


def lines_from_boxes(boxes: list) -> list[str]:
    """Group OCR boxes into text lines, top to bottom, left to right."""
    items = []
    for pts, text, conf in boxes:
        ys = [p[1] for p in pts]; xs = [p[0] for p in pts]
        items.append((sum(ys) / 4, min(xs), max(ys) - min(ys), text))
    items.sort()
    lines, cur, cur_y, cur_h = [], [], None, 0
    for y, x, h, t in items:
        if cur_y is not None and abs(y - cur_y) > max(cur_h, h) * 0.6:
            lines.append(" ".join(t for _, t in sorted(cur))); cur = []
        cur.append((x, t)); cur_y = y if cur_y is None else (cur_y + y) / 2; cur_h = h
    if cur:
        lines.append(" ".join(t for _, t in sorted(cur)))
    return lines


def split_columns(boxes: list, width: float) -> list[list]:
    """Return [left, right] if a clear vertical gutter exists near the middle, else [boxes]."""
    if len(boxes) < 12:
        return [boxes]
    mid_lo, mid_hi = width * 0.42, width * 0.58
    best = None
    for gx in np.linspace(mid_lo, mid_hi, 17):
        crossing = sum(1 for pts, _, _ in boxes if min(p[0] for p in pts) < gx < max(p[0] for p in pts))
        if best is None or crossing < best[1]:
            best = (gx, crossing)
    gx, crossing = best
    left = [b for b in boxes if max(p[0] for p in b[0]) <= gx]
    right = [b for b in boxes if min(p[0] for p in b[0]) >= gx]
    if crossing <= max(1, len(boxes) * 0.03) and len(left) >= 5 and len(right) >= 5:
        return [left, right]
    return [boxes]


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("pdf")
    ap.add_argument("--pages")
    ap.add_argument("--dpi", type=int, default=200)
    ap.add_argument("--out")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    src = Path(a.pdf)
    slug = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", src.stem.lower()).strip("-")
    out = Path(a.out) if a.out else ROOT / "staging" / "ocr" / f"{slug}.md"
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    doc = fitz.open(src)
    pages = parse_pages(a.pages, doc.page_count)
    engine = RapidOCR()
    rows, parts, t0 = [], [], time.time()
    for pno in pages:
        page = doc[pno - 1]
        pix = page.get_pixmap(dpi=a.dpi)
        img = np.frombuffer(pix.samples, dtype=np.uint8).reshape(pix.height, pix.width, pix.n)
        if pix.n == 4:
            img = img[:, :, :3]
        result, _ = engine(img)
        boxes = result or []
        text_lines = []
        for col in split_columns(boxes, pix.width):
            text_lines += lines_from_boxes(col) + [""]
        body = "\n".join(text_lines).strip()
        confs = [float(c) for _, _, c in boxes]
        mean_conf = sum(confs) / len(confs) if confs else 0.0
        rows.append({"page": pno, "words": len(body.split()), "boxes": len(boxes), "mean_conf": round(mean_conf, 3)})
        parts.append(f"<!-- page {pno} -->\n{body}")
        print(f"page {pno}: {len(body.split())} words, conf {mean_conf:.2f}", flush=True)
    low = [r["page"] for r in rows if r["boxes"] and r["mean_conf"] < LOW_CONF]
    blank = [r["page"] for r in rows if r["boxes"] == 0]
    header = (f"---\nsource: {src}\nocr: RapidOCR (onnxruntime, CPU) at {a.dpi} dpi\npages: {len(pages)}\n"
              f"low_confidence_pages: {low}\nno_text_pages: {blank}\n"
              f"note: machine OCR. Check numbers, names and tables against the page image before citing.\n---\n\n")
    out.write_text(header + "\n\n".join(parts) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    with open(out.with_suffix(".csv"), "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        w.writeheader(); w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"{out}: {len(pages)} pages in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min; low-confidence {len(low)}, blank {len(blank)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. # The 75-85% Max-Velocity Gate

**What it is** — Before progressing an athlete past roughly 75-85% of MV (Harries states the gate at "75-85%" in most places and once as "75-80%," ~13:04-16:35; the broken-stride worked example itself targets 70-75%, a step below the gate, not the gate threshold), Harries checks four things (~13:31-15:45, confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3):
1. **Time for biological healing** appropriate to the injury.
2. **Symptom response**: previous running sessions completed with minimal pain or awareness of the injured area.
3. **Force production benchmarks** in the injured area, e.g. eccentric hamstring strength via Nordic at roughly 80-85% of pre-injury baseline; seated calf isometric peak force. Harries states this two ways in the same module: as a range, "1.7 to 1.8 times body weight" (14:25-14:49), and, restated about a minute later, as a single floor, "a minimum benchmark relative to body weight such as 1.8x body weight" alongside "a minimum of 80% of pre-injury baseline outputs" for the hamstring figure (15:56-16:06). Part-3.pdf p.3 matches the floor framing for the calf number (">=1.8x bodyweight") and the range framing for the hamstring number (80-85%). Use 1.7-1.8x as the working range for the calf figure and confirm against the athlete's own baseline.
4. **Reactive strength/stretch-shortening-cycle function**, e.g. via a hopping task, to check the athlete can produce high force in a short timeframe before near-maximal speed.

The transcript checker, not Harries, marks an injury term near ~15:51 as unclear (`[injury term unclear] strain` in the source transcript); it has been left unresolved rather than guessed.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: "there are of course varied opinions in the field on this criteria, especially in regard to the assessment of force production capacities... it seems sensible to me and has almost zero downside" (~15:21-15:36). Eric's review classifies these as expert opinion, not trial results; Harries himself only says "varied opinions in the field," not that framing. Label them that way whenever they are used, and do not present the 80-85%, 1.7-1.8x, or hop-test criteria as validated thresholds.

**When to apply** — Eric's review judges this the single most transferable number in the course: a decision gate that Applied Performance can compute and hand to Athletic Medicine as a shared go/no-go check before a returning athlete is exposed to higher-velocity running. # Track Running Volume as a Percent of Game Value

**What it is** — Rather than reporting HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes as raw meters, Harries tracks and reports them as a **percent of game value** for the metric, session by session: e.g. "VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21," "sprint exposure... maybe around 50-60% of game demands," "session 8 peaked at 120% of game value" (Case 1 and 2, throughout Part 6). Harries uses "game value," "game demands," "game volume" and "match load" without ever defining the denominator; the course does not say whether it is the athlete's own historical GPS average, a club/position norm, or something else. Part 1's case-study demographic gives one athlete's per-game numbers as an example of the kind of figure a game-demand benchmark would draw on (~13 km total distance, ~1000 m HSR, ~200 m VHSR, 40-50 accels/decels per game, 34.2 km/h MV, ~02:20-02:49), but the course never states that this is how the "% of game value" denominator in the case studies was actually built.

**Why it works** — An absolute meters figure means nothing without a denominator; normalizing to "% of what this specific athlete actually does in a game" makes progress legible across the whole rehab (is this session under-, on-, or over-dosed relative to competition) and comparable across sessions and cases despite different absolute demands per position or per athlete.

**When to apply** — Build every RTP running report at Baylor around a %-of-game-value normalization so a session reads as under-, on-, or over-dosed relative to competition, rather than as a raw distance. The existing Baylor velocity-band sheet lists each position group's game averages; a per-player %-of-game-value line for a specific returning athlete is a later piece still to be built (Review and Plan, sections 3-4), not something the current sheet already reports.

**When NOT to apply** — This metric is only as good as the game-average baseline it's normalized against; a baseline built from too few games, an unrepresentative sample (e.g., mostly blowout or short-rotation games), or the wrong position comparison will distort every subsequent % figure. It is also an AFL-cohort practice built on a continuous, high-running sport; Baylor football is intermittent and position-specific, so the same %-of-game-value logic transfers, but the underlying km/h zone definitions and accel/decel counts have to be re-derived per position from Baylor's own GPS, not copied from AFL norms. Eric's review: many linemen, for instance, may rarely or never reach a comparable sprint-zone speed in a game at all, which would make a raw %-of-game-value sprint figure close to meaningless for that position without checking the baseline first.

**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]], where the same session (session 8) simultaneously showed a 120%-of-game-value peak in VHSR/sprint alongside a lower isolated-MDSA volume - both numbers only interpretable relative to that athlete's own game baseline.

**Related** — [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]; [[claim--speed-threshold-percent-of-max-velocity-conversion]]

# Confidence and Willingness Under Competitive Pressure Is Required, But Unmeasured

**What it is** — Harries requires the athlete to show restored ability, confidence and willingness to choose the right action under competitive pressure, for example "not hesitating to accelerate through a gap in the defence" (Part 2, 10:08-10:20, and see [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]). This is stated as a positive requirement to demonstrate, not as a named disqualifying red flag; hesitation is his example of what failing to meet it would look like. He never gives a way to observe, score or record it.

**Why it works** — Harries offers no mechanism, only the assertion. It is plausible on its face: hesitation under pressure plausibly reflects unresolved fear-avoidance or a lack of trust in the injured tissue. But plausibility is not the same as a defined, repeatable observation.

**When to apply** — Eric's review flags this as a real, named criterion the course itself cannot defend to an objective audience, and treats it as a legitimate prompt to look for a way to operationalize "hesitation" (a success-rate threshold on a drill, a scripted-start/live-finish task design, video-coded decision latency) rather than to rely on a coach's unaided impression. This course supplies none of those tools itself.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not write "athlete showed no hesitation" into a Baylor RTP note as if it were a measured criterion on par with the % MV or force benchmarks in [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]. It is currently an unvalidated, single-observer judgment call with no defined pass/fail rule, exactly the kind of subjective criterion the 75-85% gate's objective benchmarks were designed to avoid relying on alone.

**Example** — Two athletes both clear their force benchmarks and %MV targets; one accelerates confidently through a small-sided game gap, the other visibly slows and checks his own leg before committing. Under this criterion the second athlete would not yet meet the requirement, but the course gives no rule for how many hesitant reps, or what kind, would actually hold up a return decision.

**Related** — [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]

# Sequence Interval Length by Which Tissue Is Injured

**What it is** — Across the four case studies, Harries used two different interval-length sequencing strategies depending on injury type. Harries says hamstring rehab "might more commonly" use a **long-to-short** approach (starting with longer repeats, e.g. 100 m, and moving toward shorter, faster efforts) "to control speed" (~31:59-32:04); Cases 1 and 2 (proximal hamstring, semimembranosus/adductor) both started with 100 m repeats before moving to 60 m work, consistent with this. The recurrent calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) deliberately used the opposite, a **short-to-long** model: beginning with 60 m repeats (10-12 s efforts) and progressing to longer intervals (100 m repeats at 20-24 s, then 40 s and 60 s intervals), explicitly to control the calf's cumulative local-fatigue exposure early (~31:41-32:04).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the calf contributes disproportionately to running mechanics at all speeds (not just top speed), so short, well-spaced efforts early minimize repetitive local loading to the injured structure while still allowing systemic running-mechanics practice; longer intervals are then added once tolerance is established. For the hamstring, his stated rationale is narrower: a long-to-short approach is used "to control speed" (~32:04).

**When to apply** — When designing early on-field rehab running volume, consider the injured tissue's loading profile (does it load more with repetition frequency, as with calf, or more with peak intensity, as with hamstring at high speed) and choose interval length progression accordingly, rather than defaulting to one fixed sequencing rule for every lower-limb injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from only two data points (one calf case, two hamstring cases) inside one practitioner's own case selection; Harries never states it as a general rule, and this entry infers the generalization from the pattern across his four cases. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing against Baylor's own case data, not an established principle.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]'s 60m-then-100m-then-longer intervals against [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s early use of 100 m repeats before moving to faster 60 m work. [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] does not fit this contrast cleanly: its session 3 used 100 m repeats and its session 5 used longer 400 m repeats before returning to 60 m strides, a short-to-long sequence within a knee (not hamstring or calf) case.

**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]

# Cut Running Frequency for a Recurrent Calf Injury

**What it is** — For a recurrent lateral soleus strain, Harries deliberately ran the athlete only **twice per week**, with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions, instead of the more frequent running used in the hamstring cases. His stated reasons: "the athlete had responded well to this lower running frequency in the past" and reduced frequency/weekly load "has also been effective in some of our recurrent calf injuries that we've come across in the past" at his organization (~27:59-28:33).

**Why it works** — Harries gives three stated reasons: the athlete's own history of responding well to reduced frequency (~28:20-28:24), his organization's pattern-matched experience with other recurrent calf injuries (~28:24-28:33), and the calf's general loading profile - "the calf contributes a lot to running" on effectively every ground contact (~29:47-29:51). He does not contrast this with a hamstring-specific rationale or mention any prior re-injury under a more standard frequency for this athlete.

**When to apply** — For a recurrent (not first-time) calf/soleus strain, consider deliberately lower running frequency (e.g., twice weekly with 48+ hour gaps) as a starting strategy, especially if the athlete has a documented history of responding well to reduced frequency previously.

**When NOT to apply** — This is based on organizational pattern-matching and one athlete's own history, not a controlled comparison; it is explicitly *not* what Harries did for the hamstring cases, so do not port this frequency reduction to hamstring or other tissue types without the same recurrence-and-prior-response rationale. RTP for this case was day 44 - the second-longest of the four cases, after Case 4's 49 days - and one week of that was a deliberate delay by the medical/performance team specifically to add training exposure, not a consequence of the reduced running frequency itself (see [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]).

**Example** — See [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] for the full case; contrast with [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s six sessions across roughly the same number of weeks as this case's five sessions across a longer span.

# Sequence Interval Length by Which Tissue Is Injured

**What it is** — Across the four case studies, Harries used two different interval-length sequencing strategies depending on injury type. Harries says hamstring rehab "might more commonly" use a **long-to-short** approach (starting with longer repeats, e.g. 100 m, and moving toward shorter, faster efforts) "to control speed" (~31:59-32:04); Cases 1 and 2 (proximal hamstring, semimembranosus/adductor) both started with 100 m repeats before moving to 60 m work, consistent with this. The recurrent calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) deliberately used the opposite, a **short-to-long** model: beginning with 60 m repeats (10-12 s efforts) and progressing to longer intervals (100 m repeats at 20-24 s, then 40 s and 60 s intervals), explicitly to control the calf's cumulative local-fatigue exposure early (~31:41-32:04).

**Why it works** — Harries gives no reason for the calf's short-to-long order; the nearest remark is about high-speed running volume (~31:35-31:41). Inference: the calf contributes to running mechanics at all speeds, not just top speed, so short, well-spaced efforts early may limit repetitive local loading while still allowing running practice, with longer intervals added once tolerance is established. For the hamstring, his stated rationale is narrower: a long-to-short approach is used "to control speed" (~32:04).

**When to apply** — When designing early on-field rehab running volume, consider the injured tissue's loading profile (does it load more with repetition frequency, as with calf, or more with peak intensity, as with hamstring at high speed) and choose interval length progression accordingly, rather than defaulting to one fixed sequencing rule for every lower-limb injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from only two data points (one calf case, two hamstring cases) inside one practitioner's own case selection; Harries never states it as a general rule, and this entry infers the generalization from the pattern across his four cases. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing against Baylor's own case data, not an established principle.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]'s 60m-then-100m-then-longer intervals against [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s early use of 100 m repeats before moving to faster 60 m work. [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] does not fit this contrast cleanly: its session 3 used 100 m repeats and its session 5 used longer 400 m repeats before returning to 60 m strides, a short-to-long sequence within a knee (not hamstring or calf) case.

**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]

# Progress Max Velocity Linearly, Then Undulate Near 80-85%

**What it is** — Harries' default periodization for max-velocity exposure across sessions: increase speed session-on-session in a linear fashion through the early-to-mid part of rehab, then shift to an undulating pattern (down, up, sometimes down and back up to hold a level) once the athlete approaches roughly 80-85% of MV (~21:17-22:50; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3). His illustrative hamstring case goes linear through session 5 (50-60% -> 65-70% -> 75-80% -> 85% -> ~90-92% of MV), pushed further into the linear zone than typical (up to 90-92%) because of time pressure toward a 3-4 week return, then brings intensity down before the next jump.

**Why it works** — Harries gives the reasoning in two places. In Part 3, he says linear progression through early rehab is "quite normal and quite appropriate," and how long to stay linear before undulating "really depends on the context of the injury, how severe it was and the length of time that someone's spending in each of these on-field rehab levels" (~22:37-22:50) - a context-dependency statement, not a mechanistic one. In Part 6 (Case 1, session 6 undulation), he gives the more concrete reason: shifting to undulating "manages fatigue and the frequency of those exposures" to higher velocities (~06:43-06:46). Inference (entry writer's elaboration, not stated this way by Harries): near 80-85% MV, sessions get close enough to true maximal effort that repeating high-intensity exposures session after session could accumulate fatigue and reload risk faster than the tissue can adapt.

**When to apply** — Use linear progression as the default through on-field rehab levels 1-3 (up to ~75-85% MV), then switch to an undulating high/low pattern from roughly level 3-4 onward. How long to stay linear (and how far past 85% to push before undulating) is explicitly context-dependent on time pressure, injury severity and history, not fixed.

**When NOT to apply** — Not every case in Harries' own material follows this pattern: [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] built linearly for its first four sessions, then ran flat above 90% MV in every session from session 4 onward, with no undulating pattern, because the low running frequency (twice weekly) meant every session was already spaced far enough apart to serve as its own recovery. Do not apply the linear-then-undulate default mechanically without checking whether session frequency already provides the recovery spacing undulation is meant to create.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] and [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] (both undulated from around session 6) against [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (linear for four sessions, then flat above 90% MV, by design of its reduced frequency, not by undulation).

**Related** — [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]

# Block, Then Serial, Then Random Practice Across the Levels

**What it is** — Harries maps sport-specific skill drills onto a practice-structure continuum borrowed from motor-learning theory: **block practice** (the same drill repeated, low variability), **serial practice** (a known sequence of actions, predictable order), and **random practice** (unpredictable, variable order/decisions). He assigns these across levels (~04:03-07:26, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2-3: p.2 states the general block-to-serial-to-random progression, p.3 gives the per-level breakdown): Level 1 - solely block, tightly controlled; Level 2 - still block, intensity of the drills rises; Level 3 - roughly 50/50 block and serial, chaining action sequences; Level 4 - block dropped entirely, mostly serial with some random; Level 5 - substantial random practice, with some serial retained deliberately for actions not yet ready for full unpredictability. On return to training, levels 1-2 of training itself are "pretty much all" random.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: block-to-serial-to-random is a graded route from fully predictable to fully unpredictable practice, which lets an athlete build a skill under low cognitive/decision load first and only add decision-making demand once the movement itself is competent.

**When to apply** — Use the general shape (predictable early, unpredictable late) as the practice-structure axis alongside drill type and movement level (see [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]) when designing sport-specific skill sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Eric's review argues that block/serial/random and its associated "contextual interference effect" come from the Schmidt information-processing tradition of motor learning, not from ecological dynamics/representative learning design, which the library's skill-acquisition sources treat as the better-supported model for sport skill transfer. The practical difference: under an information-processing view, predictability itself is the variable being controlled, and the task's informational content is secondary; under an ecological view, the key variable is whether the *information* driving the action is representative of the game (a real defender, a real developing gap) regardless of how "predictable" the drill's structure is. A block-practice drill against a live, representative defender can be more transferable than a "random" drill built on arbitrary, non-representative cues. Do not assume moving along this block-serial-random axis is equivalent to moving toward game transfer; check whether the *information* in the drill, not just its unpredictability, is representative.

**Example** — Harries' own hamstring case study at Level 1 uses stationary, block-practiced kicking with the uninjured limb only (see [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]); by Level 5 it moves to a 2v1 attacking-squares game, which is "random" in his sense but still uses arbitrary defender constraints rather than a fully representative game defense.

**Related** — [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--newell-interacting-constraints]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner RTP course whose practice-structure continuum this framework's representative-design view supersedes, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]; [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Case Study: Semimembranosus Strain With Adductor Magnus Involvement (Case 2)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain, classified as "`[classification name unclear]` 2B, proximal hamstring strain with a longitudinal tendon split" (the classification system name is unclear in the audio near ~02:24 and is left unresolved here), acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. RTP day 30: six rehab-running sessions, two modified-training sessions, three full-training sessions. **The athlete returned to play one week earlier than the medical/performance team's own recommendation** - Harries flags this explicitly as "the real world nature of decision making" (~02:36-02:46).

**Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed. Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.
+## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

+- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
+- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.

+- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
+- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
+- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.
## Evidence
- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.

<system-reminder>This memory is 2 days old. Memories are point-in-time observations, not live state — claims about code behavior or file:line citations may be outdated. Verify against current code before asserting as fact.</system-reminder>
1	---
2	name: skill-bloat-and-promotion
3	description: "Measured skill bloat in this setup, the project-until-promoted rule that fixes it, and the command that re-measures usage from .jsonl session logs"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project
7	  originSessionId: f1097c6d-9db5-4bb5-a0f7-c42d645cf75d
8	  modified: 2026-09-13T06:38:22.028Z
9	---
10	
11	Measured 2026-09-12 from a gap analysis of a Nate Herk / **Mark Kashef** video
12	("How to Actually Choose the Right AI Agent", 2026-09-11). Full note:
13	`~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-harness-over-model-mark-kashef.md`.
14	Same shape as the earlier audit in [[brain-audit-loop]] — that one scored the
15	**vault**, this one scores the **skill layer**.
16	
17	## The measurement
18	
19	| Metric | Count |
20	|---|---|
21	| Global skills in `~/.claude/skills/` | 160 (→ **117** after the Tier 1 archive, 2026-09-12) |
22	| Plugin skills exposed per session | ~37 (6 enabled, 18 disabled) |
23	| SKILL.md files in plugin cache | 606 — disabled plugins + old versions, NOT the load |
24	| Project-level skills anywhere in `~/DEV` | **0** |
25	| `.jsonl` sessions scanned | 414 |
26	| Distinct real skills **ever** invoked | **58** |
27	| Used 3+ times | 30 |
28	| Used exactly once | 19 |
29	
30	Everything is global. That is the anti-pattern, not the achievement.
31	
32	## The rule that fixes it — promotion
33	
34	**Everything stays project-level until it earns global.** A skill lives in
35	`<project>/.claude/skills/` until it proves itself across 2+ projects, then it
36	gets promoted to `~/.claude/skills/`. Keeps the global load small and the blast
37	radius tight — so when something underperforms you can tell a *model* problem
38	from a *harness* problem from an *organisation* problem.
39	
40	## The audit question
41	
42	Not "how often did I run this skill?" but **"would the model do this fine without
43	the skill now?"** A skill is a crutch; as the brain gets smarter the crutch starts
44	to *limit* it. Seasonal skills (`forecast-capture`) and occasional ones
45	(`ingest-book`) are low-count by design — low usage alone is not a delete signal.
46	
47	## Re-measure (BUILTIN filter is the whole trick)
48	
49	Without the `BUILTIN` set you also count `/exit`, `/clear`, `/compact` and friends,
50	which inflates the total to 74 and buries the real skills.
51	
52	```bash
53	python3 - <<'EOF'
54	import glob,re,collections
55	BUILTIN={'exit','clear','compact','rename','color','login','logout','plugin','doctor',
56	'help','model','config','resume','cost','status','init','agents','mcp','hooks','memory',
57	'review','vim','terminal-setup','install-github-app','add-dir','bug','release-notes',
58	'pr-comments','ide','permissions','statusline','output-style','todos','export',
59	'privacy-settings','upgrade','fast','artifacts','tasks','loop','context','usage','rewind',
60	'sandbox','feedback','worktrees','skills','reload-skills','reload-plugins','bashes',
61	'keybindings','theme'}
62	c=collections.Counter()
63	for f in glob.glob('/Users/kristinarash/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl',recursive=True):
64	    try:
65	        for line in open(f,encoding='utf-8',errors='ignore'):
66	            if 'Skill' not in line and 'command-name' not in line: continue
67	            for m in re.finditer(r'"name"\s*:\s*"Skill"\s*,\s*"input"\s*:\s*\{[^}]*?"skill"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', line):
68	                c[m.group(1)]+=1
69	            for m in re.finditer(r'<command-name>/([a-zA-Z0-9:_-]+)</command-name>', line):
70	                c[m.group(1)]+=1
71	    except Exception: pass
72	real={k:v for k,v in c.items() if k.split(':')[-1] not in BUILTIN and k not in BUILTIN}
73	print("distinct real skills ever invoked:",len(real))
74	print("used >=3 times:",len([k for k,v in real.items() if v>=3]))
75	print("used exactly once:",len([k for k,v in real.items() if v==1]))
76	for k,v in sorted(real.items(),key=lambda x:-x[1]): print(f"{v:5d}  {k}")
77	EOF
78	```
79	
80	## Decision, 2026-09-12
81	
82	**Do the skill audit BEFORE adopting Pi** (`pi.dev`) as an alternative harness.
83	Rationale: the leverage is the bloat, not the harness. Auditing first means any
84	future harness move ports ~30 good skills instead of ~200 mixed ones.
85	
86	Pi facts, verified from `pi.dev/docs/latest` 2026-09-12 — full note at
87	`~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-pi-harness-research.md`:
88	
89	1. **No sandbox, no approval flows.** "Pi does not include a built-in sandbox."
90	   Project trust only guards resource *loading*, not what the agent then does.
91	   Never run Pi in `~/DEV` or near `DexaProject`. Trial it in `~/pi-trial` or a
92	   container (`sbx` keeps the credential off the container).
93	2. **Skills port for one line.** Pi implements the Agent Skills standard and already
94	   auto-discovers `~/.agents/skills/` — where 45 of the skills live. Add the rest with
95	   `{"skills": ["~/.claude/skills"]}` in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json`. It loads
96	   `AGENTS.md` **or** `CLAUDE.md` directly.
97	3. **Hooks → TypeScript extensions is a bounded port, not a rewrite** (earlier note
98	   said "weeks", that was wrong). Hooks here are already `.ts`; Pi's `tool_call` event
99	   returns `{block, reason}` — the same shape as the dcg guard.
100	4. **Claude subscription through Pi bills per token as "extra usage", NOT against plan
101	   limits.** Changes the economics of brain-swapping.
102	
103	Config lives in `~/.pi/agent/` and survives npm uninstall.
104	See also [[hook-two-copies-trap]] and [[dcg-guard-blocks]].
105	
106	## Audit outcome, 2026-09-12
107	
108	**Both tiers executed.** 99 skills archived, global **160 → 61**, roster cost
109	**19,158 → 6,428 tokens/session (a 66% cut)**. Zero regressions: none of the 99
110	had ever been invoked in 414 sessions.
111	
112	Decision 2026-09-12: keep the `mattpocock-skills` and `superpowers` **plugins** and
113	archive the local bare-name duplicates. The plugin (v1.2.3, 35 skills) ships every
114	duplicate removed and is newer than the July symlinks. Rule that follows: when a
115	plugin and a local skill share a name, **the plugin wins** — delete the local copy.
116	
117	Script: `~/.claude/skills-audit-2026-09-12.sh` (archives, never deletes — undo with
118	`mv ~/.claude/skills-archive/2026-09-12/* ~/.claude/skills/`).
119	Report: `~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-skill-audit.md`.
120	
121	Traps found while doing it:
122	1. **CORRECTED 2026-09-12 — `~/.claude/skills/` IS version-controlled.** It is its own
123	   git repo, remote `https://github.com/erash11/claude-skills.git`, and the audit was
124	   committed as `3ab4467 chore: apply global skill audit` and pushed. The earlier note
125	   that it is "gitignored, archive is the only undo" was true only of the *`dotclaude`*
126	   repo, which ignores this path — a different thing. **Git IS the safety net here, and
127	   it is also how the cut reaches Windows.** Undo with
128	   `git -C ~/.claude/skills revert <sha> && git push`, not the archive folder
129	   (`skills-archive/` is not in the repo and never reaches the other machine).
130	2. **A cut in `~/.claude/skills/` does NOT reach `~/.agents/skills/`.** After the audit,
131	   98 of the 99 archived skills were still live in the pool (306 entries there vs 61
132	   canonical). Claude Code stopped seeing them; **Pi auto-discovers that folder**, so
133	   installing Pi would have re-exposed all of them. Always cut both.
134	3. **Skills live in three places and it is easy to edit the wrong copy.**
135	   `~/.claude/skills/` (19 entries were symlinks pointing *out* to the pool),
136	   `~/.agents/skills/` (Pi, Cowork), `~/.codex/skills/` (Codex, 27 symlinks + 5 real
137	   dirs). Count with `find -L`; plain `find` undercounts.
138	4. **`sync-to-codex.sh` did `rm -rf "$dst/$s"; cp -R "$SRC/$s"`** over a 7-name
139	   allowlist. If `$SRC/$s` ever became a symlink into `$dst`, that deletes the real
140	   data. `dev-sync` tells you to run it after every pull. A `.ps1` twin has the same
141	   shape — patch both.
142	5. **`~/.claude/skills/_shared/`** holds `config.json` + `Inference/` and is resolved by
143	   10+ skills via `parents[2]/_shared/config.json`. It has **no SKILL.md**. Never treat
144	   "no SKILL.md" as "orphan, delete".
145	6. **"606 plugin skills" is cache, not load.** Only 6 of 24 plugins are enabled
146	   (~37 skills exposed). The rest are disabled plugins and old cached versions.
147	
148	## Executed 2026-09-12 — traps the live run found
149	
150	- **Views are live links now.** `~/.agents/skills/<owned>` and `~/.codex/skills/<owned>`
151	  point into canonical, so anything that writes a view path writes canonical
152	  (`graphify install --platform agents` does; see [[graphify-runtime-setup]]).
153	- **`skillOverrides` in `~/.claude/settings.json` breaks parity silently.** Codex and Pi
154	  ignore that file, so an owned skill set `"off"` there is hidden in Claude Code but live
155	  elsewhere. Perfect frontmatter does not help; `skill-portability-check.py` fails it.
156	  Resolved 2026-09-13: Eric re-enabled the 7 (ArXiv, ISA, Science, capture-insight,
157	  library-review, pp-espn, session-miner) — `~/.claude` commit `21c686d`, checker 42/42.
158	  Never set an owned skill "off" again; retire it from canonical instead.
159	- **Git's spelling wins, not the Mac's.** APFS is case-insensitive: the folder showed
160	  `Harvest` while git recorded `harvest/`. Check `git ls-files` before "fixing" a
161	  name to match the disk.
162	- **A `closeout` in another session commits your uncommitted work** (it swept Task 5's
163	  34 SKILL.md edits into its own commit). Commit each verified step immediately.
164	- **Description budget:** keep each description under ~650 chars; Claude Code caps the
165	  combined listing.
166	
167	## Architecture decided 2026-09-12 (executed through Task 5 the same day)
168	
169	**Canonical = `~/.claude/skills/`** (the git repo, real directories only, **never commit
170	a symlink** — Windows pulls this repo). `~/.agents/skills/` and `~/.codex/skills/` are
171	**generated views**, rebuilt by `sync-to-codex.sh` from a complete manifest of every
172	canonical dir holding a SKILL.md, recorded in a `.generated-by-sync-to-codex` ownership
173	file so an audit can tell a generated entry from a third-party `npx skills add` install.
174	Symlink on Mac, copy on Windows.
175	
176	Portable frontmatter contract (fires in Claude Code *and* Codex): `name` must equal the
177	directory name (TitleCase is legal), and `description` needs **both** a positive
178	"Use when …" clause with literal trigger phrases *and* a negative "Do not use …" clause.
179	Codex reads only `name` + `description` (+ optional `metadata.short-description`) and
180	ignores `argument-hint` / `allowed-tools`. Codex over-fires without the negative clause;
181	Claude will not trigger without the literal phrases.
182	
183	Plan (Codex-approved after 6 review rounds, 10→0 findings):
184	`~/DEV/KeystoneOS/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-12-harness-agnostic-aios.md`.
185	See [[dev-layout-and-discovery]], [[hook-two-copies-trap]], [[vendored-skill-install]].
186	
187	## Listing trim, 2026-09-14 (doctor-plus)
188	
189	**40 owned skills are `"name-only"` in `~/.claude/settings.json` `skillOverrides`**
190	(dotclaude commit `172d547`). 13 stay full: the ones Claude invoked itself 2+ times
191	(memory-write, CreateSkill, impeccable, claude-stack-doctor, codex-review, name-meetings,
192	project, graphify, fireflies-intake, html-to-pdf, meeting-prep, status-report) plus
193	sports-science-research-grounding. Chosen from the usage scan above (model calls vs typed).
194	
195	- Why `name-only`, not `"off"` or `disable-model-invocation`: the name stays listed, so
196	  Skill-tool chains (`startup`→`dev-sync`, `weekly-review`→`meeting-sync`) still work,
197	  the portability checker only fails `"off"`, and Codex/Pi still see full descriptions.
198	- Cost: those 40 fire less on phrases ("goodnight", "capture this"). Type `/name`.
199	- Next-session check: if ~17 local skills still show as bare names, the listing budget
200	  is being eaten by plugin skills, not these. Promote a skill back to `"on"` by deleting
201	  its line.

Measured 2026-09-12 from a gap analysis of a Nate Herk / **Mark Kashef** video
("How to Actually Choose the Right AI Agent", 2026-09-11). Full note:
`~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-harness-over-model-mark-kashef.md`.
Same shape as the earlier audit in [[brain-audit-loop]] — that one scored the
**vault**, this one scores the **skill layer**.

## The measurement

| Metric | Count |
|---|---|
| Global skills in `~/.claude/skills/` | 160 (→ **117** after the Tier 1 archive, 2026-09-12) |
| Plugin skills exposed per session | ~37 (6 enabled, 18 disabled) |
| SKILL.md files in plugin cache | 606 — disabled plugins + old versions, NOT the load |
| Project-level skills anywhere in `~/DEV` | **0** |
| `.jsonl` sessions scanned | 414 |
| Distinct real skills **ever** invoked | **58** |
| Used 3+ times | 30 |
| Used exactly once | 19 |

Everything is global. That is the anti-pattern, not the achievement.

## The rule that fixes it — promotion

**Everything stays project-level until it earns global.** A skill lives in
`<project>/.claude/skills/` until it proves itself across 2+ projects, then it
gets promoted to `~/.claude/skills/`. Keeps the global load small and the blast
radius tight — so when something underperforms you can tell a *model* problem
from a *harness* problem from an *organisation* problem.

## The audit question

Not "how often did I run this skill?" but **"would the model do this fine without
the skill now?"** A skill is a crutch; as the brain gets smarter the crutch starts
to *limit* it. Seasonal skills (`forecast-capture`) and occasional ones
(`ingest-book`) are low-count by design — low usage alone is not a delete signal.

## Re-measure (BUILTIN filter is the whole trick)

Without the `BUILTIN` set you also count `/exit`, `/clear`, `/compact` and friends,
which inflates the total to 74 and buries the real skills.

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF'
import glob,re,collections
BUILTIN={'exit','clear','compact','rename','color','login','logout','plugin','doctor',
'help','model','config','resume','cost','status','init','agents','mcp','hooks','memory',
'review','vim','terminal-setup','install-github-app','add-dir','bug','release-notes',
'pr-comments','ide','permissions','statusline','output-style','todos','export',
'privacy-settings','upgrade','fast','artifacts','tasks','loop','context','usage','rewind',
'sandbox','feedback','worktrees','skills','reload-skills','reload-plugins','bashes',
'keybindings','theme'}
c=collections.Counter()
for f in glob.glob('/Users/kristinarash/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl',recursive=True):
    try:
        for line in open(f,encoding='utf-8',errors='ignore'):
            if 'Skill' not in line and 'command-name' not in line: continue
            for m in re.finditer(r'"name"\s*:\s*"Skill"\s*,\s*"input"\s*:\s*\{[^}]*?"skill"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', line):

            for m in re.finditer(r'<command-name>/([a-zA-Z0-9:_-]+)</command-name>', line):
```

## Decision, 2026-09-12

**Do the skill audit BEFORE adopting Pi** (`pi.dev`) as an alternative harness.
Rationale: the leverage is the bloat, not the harness. Auditing first means any
future harness move ports ~30 good skills instead of ~200 mixed ones.

Pi facts, verified from `pi.dev/docs/latest` 2026-09-12 — full note at
`~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-pi-harness-research.md`:

1. **No sandbox, no approval flows.** "Pi does not include a built-in sandbox."
   Project trust only guards resource *loading*, not what the agent then does.
   Never run Pi in `~/DEV` or near `DexaProject`. Trial it in `~/pi-trial` or a
   container (`sbx` keeps the credential off the container).
2. **Skills port for one line.** Pi implements the Agent Skills standard and already
   auto-discovers `~/.agents/skills/` — where 45 of the skills live. Add the rest with
   `{"skills": ["~/.claude/skills"]}` in `~/.pi/agent/settings.json`. It loads
   `AGENTS.md` **or** `CLAUDE.md` directly.
3. **Hooks → TypeScript extensions is a bounded port, not a rewrite** (earlier note
   said "weeks", that was wrong). Hooks here are already `.ts`; Pi's `tool_call` event
   returns `{block, reason}` — the same shape as the dcg guard.
4. **Claude subscription through Pi bills per token as "extra usage", NOT against plan
   limits.** Changes the economics of brain-swapping.

Config lives in `~/.pi/agent/` and survives npm uninstall.
See also [[hook-two-copies-trap]] and [[dcg-guard-blocks]].

## Audit outcome, 2026-09-12

**Both tiers executed.** 99 skills archived, global **160 → 61**, roster cost
**19,158 → 6,428 tokens/session (a 66% cut)**. Zero regressions: none of the 99
had ever been invoked in 414 sessions.

Decision 2026-09-12: keep the `mattpocock-skills` and `superpowers` **plugins** and
archive the local bare-name duplicates. The plugin (v1.2.3, 35 skills) ships every
duplicate removed and is newer than the July symlinks. Rule that follows: when a
plugin and a local skill share a name, **the plugin wins** — delete the local copy.

Script: `~/.claude/skills-audit-2026-09-12.sh` (archives, never deletes — undo with
`mv ~/.claude/skills-archive/2026-09-12/* ~/.claude/skills/`).
Report: `~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-skill-audit.md`.

Traps found while doing it:
1. **CORRECTED 2026-09-12 — `~/.claude/skills/` IS version-controlled.** It is its own
   git repo, remote `https://github.com/erash11/claude-skills.git`, and the audit was
   committed as `3ab4467 chore: apply global skill audit` and pushed. The earlier note
   that it is "gitignored, archive is the only undo" was true only of the *`dotclaude`*
   repo, which ignores this path — a different thing. **Git IS the safety net here, and
   it is also how the cut reaches Windows.** Undo with
   `git -C ~/.claude/skills revert <sha> && git push`, not the archive folder
   (`skills-archive/` is not in the repo and never reaches the other machine).
2. **A cut in `~/.claude/skills/` does NOT reach `~/.agents/skills/`.** After the audit,
   98 of the 99 archived skills were still live in the pool (306 entries there vs 61
   canonical). Claude Code stopped seeing them; **Pi auto-discovers that folder**, so
   installing Pi would have re-exposed all of them. Always cut both.
3. **Skills live in three places and it is easy to edit the wrong copy.**
   `~/.claude/skills/` (19 entries were symlinks pointing *out* to the pool),
   `~/.agents/skills/` (Pi, Cowork), `~/.codex/skills/` (Codex, 27 symlinks + 5 real
   dirs). Count with `find -L`; plain `find` undercounts.
4. **`sync-to-codex.sh` did `rm -rf "$dst/$s"; cp -R "$SRC/$s"`** over a 7-name
   allowlist. If `$SRC/$s` ever became a symlink into `$dst`, that deletes the real
   data. `dev-sync` tells you to run it after every pull. A `.ps1` twin has the same
   shape — patch both.
5. **`~/.claude/skills/_shared/`** holds `config.json` + `Inference/` and is resolved by
   10+ skills via `parents[2]/_shared/config.json`. It has **no SKILL.md**. Never treat
   "no SKILL.md" as "orphan, delete".
6. **"606 plugin skills" is cache, not load.** Only 6 of 24 plugins are enabled
   (~37 skills exposed). The rest are disabled plugins and old cached versions.

## Executed 2026-09-12 — traps the live run found

- **Views are live links now.** `~/.agents/skills/<owned>` and `~/.codex/skills/<owned>`
  point into canonical, so anything that writes a view path writes canonical
  (`graphify install --platform agents` does; see [[graphify-runtime-setup]]).
- **`skillOverrides` in `~/.claude/settings.json` breaks parity silently.** Codex and Pi
  ignore that file, so an owned skill set `"off"` there is hidden in Claude Code but live
  elsewhere. Perfect frontmatter does not help; `skill-portability-check.py` fails it.
  Resolved 2026-09-13: Eric re-enabled the 7 (ArXiv, ISA, Science, capture-insight,
  library-review, pp-espn, session-miner) — `~/.claude` commit `21c686d`, checker 42/42.
  Never set an owned skill "off" again; retire it from canonical instead.
- **Git's spelling wins, not the Mac's.** APFS is case-insensitive: the folder showed
  `Harvest` while git recorded `harvest/`. Check `git ls-files` before "fixing" a
  name to match the disk.
- **A `closeout` in another session commits your uncommitted work** (it swept Task 5's
  34 SKILL.md edits into its own commit). Commit each verified step immediately.
- **Description budget:** keep each description under ~650 chars; Claude Code caps the
  combined listing.

## Architecture decided 2026-09-12 (executed through Task 5 the same day)

**Canonical = `~/.claude/skills/`** (the git repo, real directories only, **never commit
a symlink** — Windows pulls this repo). `~/.agents/skills/` and `~/.codex/skills/` are
**generated views**, rebuilt by `sync-to-codex.sh` from a complete manifest of every
canonical dir holding a SKILL.md, recorded in a `.generated-by-sync-to-codex` ownership
file so an audit can tell a generated entry from a third-party `npx skills add` install.
Symlink on Mac, copy on Windows.

Portable frontmatter contract (fires in Claude Code *and* Codex): `name` must equal the
directory name (TitleCase is legal), and `description` needs **both** a positive
"Use when …" clause with literal trigger phrases *and* a negative "Do not use …" clause.
Codex reads only `name` + `description` (+ optional `metadata.short-description`) and
ignores `argument-hint` / `allowed-tools`. Codex over-fires without the negative clause;
Claude will not trigger without the literal phrases.

Plan (Codex-approved after 6 review rounds, 10→0 findings):
`~/DEV/KeystoneOS/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-12-harness-agnostic-aios.md`.
See [[dev-layout-and-discovery]], [[hook-two-copies-trap]], [[vendored-skill-install]].

## Listing trim, 2026-09-14 (doctor-plus)

**40 owned skills are `"name-only"` in `~/.claude/settings.json` `skillOverrides`**
(dotclaude commit `172d547`). 13 stay full: the ones Claude invoked itself 2+ times
(memory-write, CreateSkill, impeccable, claude-stack-doctor, codex-review, name-meetings,
project, graphify, fireflies-intake, html-to-pdf, meeting-prep, status-report) plus
sports-science-research-grounding. Chosen from the usage scan above (model calls vs typed).

- Why `name-only`, not `"off"` or `disable-model-invocation`: the name stays listed, so
  Skill-tool chains (`startup`→`dev-sync`, `weekly-review`→`meeting-sync`) still work,
  the portability checker only fails `"off"`, and Codex/Pi still see full descriptions.
- Cost: those 40 fire less on phrases ("goodnight", "capture this"). Type `/name`.
- Next-session check: if ~17 local skills still show as bare names, the listing budget
  is being eaten by plugin skills, not these. Promote a skill back to `"on"` by deleting
  its line.

1	"""Extract a PDF into per-page text as JSON, and detect scanned/image PDFs.
2	Usage: python extract_pdf.py <book.pdf> [--pages A-B] [--probe]
3	Prefers pypdf; if absent, attempts pip install into user site at runtime.
4	--probe prints {"pages": N, "text_pages": K, "scanned": bool} and exits.
5	"""
6	import sys, json, subprocess
7	
8	def _ensure_pypdf():
9	    try:
10	        import pypdf  # noqa
11	        return
12	    except ImportError:
13	        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "--quiet", "--user", "pypdf"], check=False)
14	
15	def load(path):
16	    _ensure_pypdf()
17	    from pypdf import PdfReader
18	    return PdfReader(path)
19	
20	def page_texts(reader):
21	    out = []
22	    for pg in reader.pages:
23	        try: out.append(pg.extract_text() or "")
24	        except Exception: out.append("")
25	    return out
26	
27	def main():
28	    args = sys.argv[1:]
29	    if not args:
30	        print("usage: extract_pdf.py <book.pdf> [--pages A-B] [--probe]", file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(2)
31	    path = args[0]
32	    reader = load(path)
33	    texts = page_texts(reader)
34	    if "--probe" in args:
35	        text_pages = sum(1 for t in texts if len(t.strip()) > 40)
36	        n = len(texts)
37	        scanned = n > 0 and (text_pages / n) < 0.2
38	        print(json.dumps({"pages": n, "text_pages": text_pages, "scanned": scanned}))
39	        return
40	    lo, hi = 0, len(texts)
41	    if "--pages" in args:
42	        rng = args[args.index("--pages") + 1]
43	        a, b = rng.split("-")
44	        lo, hi = int(a), int(b)
45	    print(json.dumps([{"page": i, "text": texts[i]} for i in range(lo, min(hi, len(texts)))], ensure_ascii=False))
46	
47	if __name__ == "__main__":
48	    main()

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.
